## SITE-hiacsgdb: Layer E hreflang never reads the Link header (port from sitemap-validator)

**Status:** done | **Parent:** nlptpmdqqvmldzbdrfwhwlceepjoksne

### Description

### Claim

`page_hreflang_extract()` sources its alternate set solely from the HTML head. A page declaring its alternates in the HTTP `Link` header — `Link: <https://example.com/de>; rel="alternate"; hreflang="de"` — is treated as having declared none.

`R/page-hreflang.R:111`:

```r
html <- page_hreflang_html_links(art$body, art$final_url)
set  <- page_hreflang_norm_set(html$links, html$base)
```

`terminal_headers` appears nowhere in `R/page-hreflang.R`.

This is inconsistent **within sitemapr itself**: `page-canonical.R` already consults the header via `page_link_header_canonicals()`, and `page-canonical.R:17` describes both channels as the declaration methods. Canonical reads the header; hreflang does not.

### Why it matters

The header form is the only way to declare alternates for a non-HTML resource, and Google treats HTML link elements, `Link` headers and sitemap `<xhtml:link>` as equivalent methods. Because the set-vs-set rule only fires when both sides declared something, the effect today is a **silent miss**, not a false positive: a header-only page reads as 'no alternates observed' and a genuine page/sitemap disagreement goes unreported.

### Provenance — the sibling now does this

sitemap-validator SMV-jyhjaqno (commit `eb9c790`) added `Link` header parsing for **both** canonical and hreflang. Reproduced there first: a page serving `Link: <…/fr>; rel="alternate"; hreflang="fr"` against a sitemap declaring `de`/`en` produced `hreflangLinks: []` and no `PAGE_HREFLANG_MISMATCH`; after the fix the mismatch fires.

Its precedence decision, for reference: **union, not override** — a page may legitimately split its alternates across the two methods, and since each link is keyed through the canonical loc key, a target declared both ways collapses to one entry rather than counting twice.

### Step 1 — Verify before coding (REQUIRED)

Per the epic rule. Construct an artifact whose `terminal_headers` carry a `rel="alternate"; hreflang=…` link-value and whose body declares no alternates; confirm `page_hreflang_extract()` returns an empty set and that a disagreeing sitemap declaration produces no finding.

### Notes

- Do not reuse `page_link_header_canonicals()` as-is — it has two `rel`-matching defects, filed separately as a sibling issue. A shared, corrected link-value parser serving both producers is the better shape.
- RFC 8288 permits `hreflang` to appear more than once in a single link-value, each occurrence declaring another language for the same target.
- No finding code changes: this feeds the existing `PAGE_HREFLANG_MISMATCH` input.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

VERIFIED then FIXED at e3124ef (local only -- GitHub account still suspended).

Step 1 reproduced the claim exactly as filed, including the silent-miss framing: an artifact whose terminal_headers carried 'Link: <https://example.com/de>; rel="alternate"; hreflang="de"' with a body declaring no alternates returned set = character(0) and status `absent`, and against a sitemap declaring `fr` produced NO finding. The same alternates moved into the head fired PAGE_HREFLANG_MISMATCH, so the reconciliation predicate itself was fine -- the channel was simply absent.

Followed both notes in the issue:
- Did NOT reuse page_link_header_canonicals() as-is. Its two rel defects were fixed first under SITE-dsdkjvyw by extracting a shared RFC 8288 parser (R/page-link-header.R); this commit consumes the same parser, so canonical and hreflang cannot drift on link-value semantics.
- 3.4's repeatable hreflang is handled: one (tag, href) link per hreflang parameter occurrence within a single link-value, pinned by a test (hreflang=de; hreflang=de-AT -> two links, same target).

Adopted the sibling's UNION-not-override precedence, and the keying makes it collapse rather than double-count -- both pinned: head=de + header=fr -> a 2-element set that AGREES with a sitemap declaring both (either channel alone would have disagreed); head=de + header=DE -> 1 element.

Two decisions the issue did not specify, both recorded in code comments:
- Header targets resolve against the response final_url, NOT a <base href> from the body. A <base> governs the body's links only. Tested with a <base href> pointing at a different origin, which the header link correctly ignores.
- A `partial` body still returns `unknown`. The header set is complete, but the page may declare more below the body's cut, so the union is incomplete too -- the 4 safety argument for the early return is unchanged. Left it alone deliberately.

Side effect worth noting: a NON-HTML resource can now reach status `observed`, since the header is the only channel it has. Previously any non-HTML body fell to not_applicable. Tested with an application/pdf artifact.

Docs: docs/design/layer-e-page-inspection.md described hreflang as reading the 'artifact body' (2 table) and the page 'head' (4 facts). Both now name the two channels and the union rule; 5.2 records the shared parser and the token-list rel.

## SITE-hwemiqne: Text line-splitting is ~270x slower than it needs to be (perl = TRUE strsplit)

**Status:** done

### Description

### Claim (VERIFIED before filing, on this session's measurements)

Splitting a text document into lines with `strsplit(s, "\\r\\n|\\r|\\n", perl = TRUE)` is quadratic-ish in PCRE and dominates the whole text validation path.

Measured on a 50,000-line text sitemap (each line `https://example.com/pN`):

| stage | time |
|---|---|
| `validate_text_protocol()` total | 19.3 s |
| the single `strsplit(..., perl = TRUE)` inside it | **18.6 s** |
| `loc_absoluteness()` | 0.01 s |
| `text_absolute_hosts()` (one rurl parse over 50k) | 0.65 s |
| `text_duplicate_findings()` | 0.10 s |
| `trimws()` + `nzchar()` over 50k | 0.01 s |

Dropping `perl = TRUE` produces a **byte-identical** result in **0.07 s** — a ~270x speedup:

    perl = TRUE       18.7 s  n = 50000
    default (TRE)      0.07 s  n = 50000
    perl + useBytes   18.8 s  n = 50000

The pattern is a plain three-way alternation of literals with no PCRE-only syntax, so TRE and PCRE agree on it by construction; `useBytes` does not help, which rules out an encoding-conversion explanation.

### Scope

Five call sites use the same `"\\r\\n|\\r|\\n"` + `perl = TRUE` idiom:

- `R/parse-text.R:105` (`parse_sitemap_text()`)
- `R/protocol-validate.R:2051` (`validate_text_protocol()`)
- `R/validate-sitemap.R:828` (the robots part on the text branch)
- `R/robots.R:43`
- `R/probe.R:106`

The first three all run on the SAME document in one `validate_sitemap()` call, so a 50k text sitemap pays the cost roughly three times.

### Why it matters

This lands directly on the feature just shipped in SITE-lcmvzpel: a document large enough to trip `PROTOCOL_URL_COUNT_EXCEEDED` is exactly the document that takes ~19 s per split to report it. It is the same class as the Layer D 50k perf work (PRs #72/#73) — a per-document hot path with an accidental super-linear factor.

### Approach

Drop `perl = TRUE` at the five sites. Consider folding the idiom into one shared helper (`split_lines()`) so there is a single place to reason about line-ending semantics and one place for the perf note.

Verify equality rather than assuming it: for each site, assert the old and new splits are `identical()` over the existing fixtures (CRLF, lone-CR, mixed, BOM, trailing newline, empty document) before swapping.

### Caution

`R/probe.R` is one of the five files with `air format` drift (SITE-dxujycqe) — touching it drags unrelated argument-wrapping churn into the diff. Either land SITE-dxujycqe first or leave probe.R for last.

### Done

All five sites split without PCRE; a 50,000-line text sitemap validates in well under a second of split time; equality with the previous behavior is asserted, not assumed.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Fixed in dff1c85 (local; GitHub still suspended, unpushed).

### Reproduced first, at 2e2464c

Claim held up almost exactly as filed. On a 50,000-line document:

    perl = TRUE        17.40s   n=50000
    TRE (default)       0.06s   n=50000
    perl + useBytes    17.85s   n=50000
    identical(perl, TRE): TRUE

~290x. useBytes does not help, confirming it is not encoding conversion.

### Equality asserted, not assumed

Both engines compared over 22 inputs before any swap: LF / CRLF / lone-CR / mixed, leading + trailing + doubled separators, whitespace-only, tabs, no-break-at-all, 100k-char single line, multibyte UTF-8, emoji, UTF-8 BOM, latin1-declared, and invalid UTF-8. MISMATCHES: 0.

Invalid UTF-8 is the only interesting case: both engines warn and return the input unsplit. Only the warning WORDING differs (PCRE says 'input string 1 is invalid UTF-8', TRE says 'unable to translate ... to a wide string'). Behavior is identical; no test asserts on that text.

### Change

All five sites now call one split_lines() helper in R/parse-text.R - the single place the line-ending rule is stated and the single place the engine choice is justified. Sites: parse-text.R, protocol-validate.R, validate-sitemap.R, robots.R, probe.R.

Left on PCRE deliberately (not line-splitting): page-canonical.R:88 uses a lookahead, which is PCRE-only; parse-archive.R:167 splits a path on a character class.

### End-to-end result

    validate_sitemap() on 50k-line text sitemap:  19.3s -> 0.80s
    read_sitemap():                                       0.09s (50000 rows)
    50,001 lines -> PROTOCOL_URL_COUNT_EXCEEDED:          0.79s

The last line is the point: the count cap shipped in SITE-lcmvzpel is now reportable at speed on exactly the documents that trip it.

### Done criteria

All five sites off PCRE: YES. 50k splits in well under a second: YES (0.06s split, 0.80s whole validation). Equality asserted: YES, 22 cases, 10 pinned as a regression test plus a timing ceiling.

### Gates

Suite 0 failures (one pre-existing OSS Index skip). lint clean. Coverage 100.00%. check-docs + check-findings-registry OK (93/72, untouched). Corpus golden re-derived, unchanged.

## SITE-hxzmvlkn: ADR-008 concurrency scheduler dispatches sequentially — no requests overlap

**Status:** done | **Parent:** nlptpmdqqvmldzbdrfwhwlceepjoksne

### Description

### Claim

The ADR-008 bounded-concurrency scheduler does not actually overlap requests. `R/index-expansion.R:459-471`:

```r
    inflight_probe_note(length(batch))
    for (url in batch) {
      acc$fetch_cache[[url]] <- list(
        crec = tryCatch(fetch_source(url, ...), error = function(e) NULL)
      )
    }
```

That is a sequential `for` loop over `httr2::req_perform()` (`R/fetch.R:749`) inside a windowing loop. `DESCRIPTION` Imports reportedly carry no `curl`, `mirai`, `future`, or `promises`, and there is no `req_perform_parallel()`. The scheduler windows requests but never overlaps them — the `max_active` cap is honoured trivially because in-flight count is always 1.

The page-inspection loop has the same shape (`R/page-inspect.R:215-238`).

`sitemap-validator` does real concurrent fetching: `Promise.all` with a per-host semaphore (`src/lib/services/inspection/inspector.ts:33-74, 182`).

### Step 1 — Verify before coding (REQUIRED)

1. Read `fetch_batch_into_cache()` end to end and confirm the dispatch is sequential.
2. Check `DESCRIPTION` Imports/Suggests for any parallel HTTP capability.
3. **Measure it.** Time an index expansion with N children against a slow endpoint; if wall-clock is ~N×latency, the loop is sequential. This is the only check that settles it.
4. Confirm the ADR-008 design intent — if it explicitly scoped itself to windowing-only for a first pass, this is unfinished work rather than a defect, and the issue should be reframed. Record which.

### Why it matters

This is the single largest wall-clock win available to sitemapr, and the surrounding machinery is already built for it: the completion-order permutation seam (`R/index-expansion.R:387-402`) and the in-flight peak probe (`:404-415`) exist precisely to validate a concurrent implementation, and would exercise it on day one.

### Approach

`httr2::req_perform_parallel()` is a `curl::multi` wrapper and httr2 is already an Import, so it adds no new hard dependency — try that first. Preserve the byte-identical-output guarantee: results must commit in a deterministic order regardless of completion order, which the existing seam is designed to test.

Apply to index-expansion child prefetch first, then page inspection.

### Files

- `R/index-expansion.R` — `fetch_batch_into_cache()`
- `R/page-inspect.R` — page fetch loop
- `R/fetch.R`
- `DESCRIPTION`

### Done

Requests genuinely overlap up to `max_active` (proven by the in-flight probe and by wall-clock); output is byte-identical across completion-order permutations; the SSRF per-hop guard still runs on every redirect.


### Comments

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Step 1 verification: claim REPRODUCED, and understated.

Measured against a threaded local HTTP server with a 300ms fixed delay that
counts its OWN observed concurrency (client self-reporting is not trusted).
N=8 requests, max_active=4. Sequential would be ~2.40s, overlapped ~0.60s.

  A. httr2::req_perform_parallel(max_active=4): 0.94s, server peak = 5
  B. bare sequential req_perform loop:          2.46s, server peak = 1
  C. sitemapr fetch_batch_into_cache(cap=4):    2.50s, server peak = 1

C/B = 1.02. sitemapr is exactly as slow as a sequential loop; server-observed
peak concurrency is 1. Real concurrency on the same server is 2.7x faster.

Step 2: DESCRIPTION Imports carry httr2 only -- no curl/mirai/future/promises,
no req_perform_parallel call anywhere. Confirmed.

Step 4: ADR-008 did NOT scope itself to windowing-only. Its 'Next step'
section requires the scheduler to drive 'httr2::req_perform_parallel() (or an
equivalent bounded worker pool)', and SITE-tktfxoxe's own Done criterion reads
'configured concurrency reduces wall-clock time in a controlled integration
benchmark'. That criterion was never met. This is UNFINISHED WORK, not a
defect against a deliberate first-pass scope: the determinism half of ADR-008
shipped and is genuinely validated, the dispatch half did not.

NEW FINDING, not in the claim -- the validation instrument is vacuous.
inflight_probe_note(length(batch)) reports the INTENDED window size, not
observed in-flight count. In run C the probe reported peak = 4 while the
server observed 1. So test-concurrency-contract.R:304,
expect_gt(probe$peak_inflight(), 1L), reads as 'requests genuinely overlap'
but passes on a fully sequential path. That false-green is how this shipped as
done. Any fix must re-point the probe at observed concurrency, or the day-one
validation this issue promises stays hollow.

Methodology note: the first run of this measurement was INVALID and looked
fast (0.02s). The SSRF mock returned list(blocked=FALSE) but the contract is
check$allowed, so all 8 fetches aborted and tryCatch swallowed it. Only the
server-side request counter caught it. The script now hard-fails unless all N
fetches return non-NULL records.

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Fixed in 8190dd5 (local; GitHub account still suspended, nothing pushed).

fetch_batch_follow() -- an ADDITIVE parallel sibling of the frozen
fetch_follow(), reusing its ADR-003 primitives rather than reimplementing
them. Redirects are followed in ROUNDS: guard every active URL, hand the whole
round to httr2::req_perform_parallel(), advance one hop. So the per-hop SSRF
guard still precedes every request and a redirect cannot skip a check --
the ADR-003 ordering is structurally preserved, not re-asserted by hand.
fetch_perform_one() was split into fetch_build_request() + perform so both
schedulers build requests from ONE definition; a request whose transport
controls varied by dispatcher would breach §0 on its own.

Determinism: responses are collected during the rounds but NO record is built
until every URL is terminal, then records are assembled in catalog order. That
pins both the returned order and the order in which a non-2xx emits its
sitemapr_http_error warning, whatever order the pool completed in.

Per-URL failure isolation: SSRF block, redirect limit, transport failure and
body ceiling each retire that URL alone as a NULL record -- exactly what the
sequential path's caught abort already became at this call site -- rather than
tearing down the batch. No https->http fallback is needed: it fires only for
an inferred scheme, and no batch caller passes one.

MEASURED after, same rig as the verification (N=8, 300ms, cap=4):

  before: 2.50s, server-observed peak 1
  after:  0.99s, server-observed peak 5
  raw httr2::req_perform_parallel control: 0.95s, peak 5

2.5x faster, and within 5% of the bare primitive. Server-side counting, so the
overlap is observed from outside the process, not self-reported.

Done criteria:
- requests genuinely overlap up to max_active -- yes, wall-clock + server peak
- byte-identical across completion-order permutations -- yes, the existing
  contract tests pass untouched
- per-hop SSRF guard on every redirect -- yes, structurally, plus a new test
  that a blocked child retires alone while its siblings still fetch
- default max_active=1 still skips prefetch entirely, so the sequential path
  is byte-identical; corpus golden re-derived and unmoved (corpus fixtures are
  local files that never enter the network prefetch path)

Also corrected the false-green test this issue's verification exposed. The
probe now reports dispatch width, and test-concurrency-contract.R says plainly
that mocked responses cannot demonstrate real overlap and that the wall-clock
evidence lives here.

Gates: full suite 0 failures (1 pre-existing OSS Index skip), lint clean,
coverage 100.00%, check-docs + findings-registry green (93/72, nothing
minted). DESCRIPTION floors httr2 to >= 1.1.1, the release that added
max_active.

DEFERRED, filed as SITE-rjhmkqnd: the 'then page inspection' half. Not a
mechanical repeat -- page_inspection_cap_hit() breaks on CUMULATIVE bytes and
elapsed seconds, which ADR-008 §3's reserve-before-dispatch cannot cover
(neither is knowable before the fetch). Concurrency there would change which
pages are sampled when a cap trips mid-batch, an observable output change with
no accepted decision behind it. Page inspection has no max_active knob today,
so nothing regresses by leaving it sequential.

## SITE-ibeevjwt: Cross-port divergence: image:caption/title rejected by sitemapr's image XSD

**Status:** done

### Description

Surfaced by the imported validator corpus (SITE-uivyzfhe). validate_sitemap('corpus/xml/valid-image.xml') returns SCHEMA_INVALID: 'Element <caption> in the image namespace scope failed XSD schema validation.' sitemapr's bundled image profile only accepts <image:loc> (Google removed image:caption/title/geo_location/license from the image sitemap spec in 2022), whereas sitemap-validator's fixture still uses <image:title>/<image:caption> and treats them as valid. Decide the canonical behavior across ports: either (a) sitemapr is correct per current spec and the validator fixture/schema is stale, or (b) accept the legacy fields for backward-compat. Whichever, align both ports + the shared golden reference. Ref: fixtures/corpus/xml/valid-image.xml, fixtures/corpus-golden.tsv.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-04 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Resolved (PR #89, squash-merged to main as 824ad92).

DECISION: sitemapr is canonical — option (a). The issue premise was inaccurate: sitemapr's bundled image XSD already accepts caption/geo_location/title/license. The actual divergence is CHILD ORDER. Fetched Google's LIVE upstream image XSD (www.google.com/schemas/sitemap-image/1.1/sitemap-image.xsd) — it models <image:image> as an xsd:sequence: loc -> caption -> geo_location -> title -> license. The validator fixture valid-image.xml orders <title> before <caption>, which is genuinely SCHEMA_INVALID per Google. sitemapr is faithful to upstream, so its verdict is correct.

No schema/fixture/golden change in sitemapr: it already emits SCHEMA_INVALID and the shared golden (corpus-golden.tsv) records it; the corpus stays byte-identical to the validator per fixtures/COPYRIGHTS. Instead:
- docs/sitemap-spec.md §5/§5.1: disambiguated 'order is irrelevant' (sibling extension blocks only, not children within a block) and documented the significant image child-order sequence + this cross-port decision.
- helper-schema-corpus.R: added a negative case (loc, title, caption) matching the fixture shape, locking the rule against both the bundled schema (test-schema-conformance, 43 pass) and live upstream (check-parity oracle).

CROSS-PORT FOLLOW-UP (not actionable in this repo): sitemap-validator should fix the ordering in — or rename — its valid-image.xml fixture and ensure its schema enforces the sequence. Owned in the sibling sitemap-validator repo.

#### 2026-07-04 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Cross-port follow-up tracked as SITE-mymellmc (sitemapr-side mirror reminder). The validator-side fix itself is owned in the sibling sitemap-validator repo under the SMV- prefix, which is not reachable from this SITE-scoped fp instance.

## SITE-ihycidfl: v0.2: per-URL page inspection (Layer E)

**Status:** done

### Description

**Epic: v0.2 per-URL page inspection (Layer E).** Opt-in, budgeted, engine-aware `page`-layer inspection over the registered `PAGE_*` codes.

**Governing contract:** `docs/design/layer-e-page-inspection.md` (promoted from `_scratch/` and hardened; §0 is authoritative over the v2.1 body). Goals/non-goals/acceptance in §0.2.

### Architecture — three layers (§0.1)
- **Access** (robots.txt, engine-aware) — sitemap doc + listed URLs; owned by `robotstxtr`.
- **Fetch** (server+URL, **engine-neutral**) — E.1a; engine identity must not leak in.
- **Interpretation** (per-engine) — E.2/E.3/E.4.

### Settled decisions (§0)
- **Crawler-token axis** → adopt `robotstxtr` engine-contract-v1 (`robots_product_token`/`robots_policy_ruleset`/`matcher_backend` + `token_policy`); **no new ADR-009 axis**. *Use* it for access (E.5/E.1b/sitemap-check); *steal the ideas* for interpretation (E.3) — interpretation must degrade without the `Suggests` `robotstxtr`.
- **`partial`** → the page-inspection ADR **amends ADR-009 §2** (not a cross-ref).
- **Transport severities** → conform to `findings-registry.csv` (`PAGE_STATUS_REDIRECT=warning`, `PAGE_REDIRECT_CHAIN=info`); 500 MB ceiling → `PAGE_FETCH_FAILED`, not `PAGE_SSRF_BLOCKED`.
- **Findings encoding** → per-finding `context` merge in engine mode; `evidence$excerpt` fallback on the ten-column baseline; `remediation_hint` pass-through.
- **New check** → sitemap document blocked by robots.txt (robots layer, E.5 sibling).

### Status
- **Done:** E.5 (SITE-ofdqaeju); report-layer fix (SITE-lwvktkte).
- **Prep (no deps):** ADR (SITE-ndwnfyer), fold-doc (SITE-makpbnan), assembler (SITE-qvdjvwwy), **E.1b implementable now** (SITE-kwkggijf).
- **Fetch infra:** E.1a artifact (SITE-agfcwgmh) → E.1s selection/budget (SITE-rtbonaev) → E.1f findings/coverage/params (SITE-apmcsvqb).
- **Extractors (→ E.1f):** E.2 canonical (SITE-eoqgkcij), E.3 noindex+trap (SITE-weonydlw), E.4 hreflang (SITE-dqbbbkja).
- **Robots sibling:** sitemap-blocked check (SITE-zfggbgsj, → E.1b).
- **Non-gating / related:** cross-repo tail SITE-wrylygzd (detached); empirical meta-vs-header test SITE-dbcjeouj; `indexationr` idea ROBO-lhwpffij.

### Dependency spine
ADR → E.1a → E.1s → E.1f → {E.2, E.3, E.4}. E.3 also needs E.1b; E.2/E.3/E.4 also need the assembler + fold-doc. ADR/fold-doc/assembler/E.1b have no deps.

## SITE-iqqoekjk: Page fetch: HTTPS→HTTP downgrade rejection → safety_refused (E.1a follow-up)

**Status:** done | **Parent:** ihycidflmgtcvnctecfqldgdulicucex

### Description

Spec §3.2 + ADR-010 §3 name an HTTPS→HTTP downgrade rejection as one of the three safety_refused classes (alongside SSRF address + non-HTTP(S) scheme). E.1a (SITE-agfcwgmh) deferred it: the reused ADR-003 SSRF guard has NO downgrade-rejection mechanism, and adding one is non-trivial because it must NOT collide with the deliberate inferred-scheme http FALLBACK at R/fetch.R:797 (a bare-domain entrypoint may legitimately fall back https→http).

Scope: in page_fetch_follow() (R/fetch.R), detect a redirect hop whose scheme steps down from https to http for a NON-inferred-scheme request, map to outcome=safety_refused (prefix discarded, no page verdict). Add offline tests.

Ordering: close BEFORE or WITH E.1f (SITE-apmcsvqb), which maps safety_refused → PAGE_SSRF_BLOCKED — until then a downgrade is silently followed as a normal hop and never flagged.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-20 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Done — PR #169, squash-merged as main 778cc76, branch deleted local+remote.

page_hop_is_downgrade() in R/fetch.R; page_fetch_follow() aborts
sitemapr_scheme_downgrade, page_fetch() maps it to safety_refused. E.1f's
existing safety_refused -> PAGE_SSRF_BLOCKED mapping picks it up, so no new
finding code and the registry is unchanged (94 codes / 71 active).

The stated collision risk with the inferred-scheme https->http fallback at
R/fetch.R:797 turned out to be structurally absent: that fallback is a
connection-failure retry on the frozen fetch_source() path, never a redirect
hop, and page inspection has no scheme inference (page URLs are advertised
<loc>s with explicit schemes). So the rejection is unconditional inside
page_fetch_follow(), with the rationale recorded in design section 3.2
(marked DELIVERED).

Ordering: downgrade check precedes the redirect-cap check, per ADR-010 section
3 safety-over-resource precedence. The hop that issued the downgrading Location
is recorded before the abort; the refused target is never requested.

Also noted: the issue's "close before or with E.1f" ordering was stale (E.1f
already done), so the gap was live rather than pending.

Verify gate green: R CMD check --as-cran 0 errors / 0 warnings / 1 baseline
NOTE, lint clean, docs reproducible. 6 new offline tests.

Revised host plan vs the 2026-07-19 comment: the lab is served by the **worker**, not by Cloudflare Pages Functions. That drops the Pages deploy (and therefore the GitHub dependency — wrangler deploys from local, so the account suspension does not block this) and keeps status-controllability, which was the original reason for choosing Functions.

**Design — the attribution invariant**

Every probe page is reachable through exactly ONE discovery channel; root pages link to nothing and no fixture repeats another fixture's pages. So "page X was fetched" identifies the channel, and the access-log user-agent identifies the engine. Most conclusions are therefore readable from server logs alone, independent of what a webmaster console chooses to report. The check script fails if any page ever gains a second channel.

45 probe pages across 8 probe families: fetch-status (6 statuses, byte-identical valid sitemap, status is the only variable), content-type (4), format (Atom 0.3 / Atom 1.0 / RSS 2.0 / TXT / gzip), directory-scope (two identical fixtures on disjoint channels — robots.txt vs console submission — which is what separates the waiver's "validity vs downgrade" question), cross-site (authorised via the secondary's robots.txt handshake, plus an unvouched control), priority, changefreq, lastmod. Pages serve Last-Modified and answer If-Modified-Since with 304, so revalidation is distinguishable from re-fetch for the recrawl probes.

Verified locally: `wrangler deploy --dry-run` builds; the check script passes all 25 fixture routes, gzip magic bytes, 304 revalidation, and the attribution invariant; `wrangler dev --host sitemap-lab.turczynski.pl` confirms worker.js dispatch end to end.

**Protocol**

`_scratch/prod-engine-tests/PROTOCOL.md` — deployment steps, per-engine submission checklist (tier 1 = the questions this issue asks; tier 2 = format/content-type surface), the Analytics Engine SQL for reading crawls, per-probe observation matrices with OBSERVED columns and reading guides, and a final contrast pass against the tester findings in _scratch/per-engine-profile-review/yandex-url-length-probe/FINDINGS.md. Includes teardown.

## SITE-klcowlkl: Port PAGE_CANONICAL_RELATIVE: implement the §4 relative/fragment facts and interpret them

**Status:** done

### Description

Ported from the sibling TypeScript implementation (sitemap-validator), which
minted the code. Cross-port contract: ADR-009 §7 — finding codes are shared, and
the validator's counterpart record is `SMV-dhrpsgvo`.

### Framing: an interpretation of a fact §4 already mandates, not a new concept

`docs/design/layer-e-page-inspection.md` §4 ("Contract B — raw-facts schema, pure
extraction, no interpretation") requires each canonical fact to carry "the raw
target, **whether it was relative** (and its resolved absolute form against the
response base / `<base>`), and any fragment".

The implementation did not do that: fact records were only
`list(channel=, raw=, resolved=)`. So `relative` and `fragment` were both
**unimplemented contract items**, and the finding is the interpretation of the
first of them.

### What landed

- `page_canonical_is_relative()` — the §4 `relative` fact. Lexical scheme test
  per RFC 3986 §3.1, deliberately **not** `parse_url_adapter()$scheme`: rurl
  *infers* `http` for a scheme-less `example.com/b`, which is right for an
  advertised loc and wrong for this fact. The lexical test also matches the
  sibling port, where `new URL(raw)` throws for exactly these forms.
- `page_canonical_fragment()` — the §4 `fragment` fact. NA when absent, `""` for
  a bare `#`. A fact only: ADR-005 drops the fragment from the comparison key.
- `PAGE_CANONICAL_RELATIVE` (info, page, page-url, baseline) in
  `docs/findings-registry.csv`, with `validator_code` aliased to the same string.
- `page_canonical_relative_finding()`. Fires on status `observed` when any
  occurrence was relative — **independent of the consistency verdict**, so a
  relative canonical resolving to exactly the advertised loc still carries it and
  one resolving elsewhere earns both codes. `page_canonical_one_finding()` was
  split into a consistency producer + this one and may now return two rows.
- Both channels: a `Link` header canonical may be a relative URI-Reference
  (RFC 8288), and it is reported too.

### Severity and ruleset

`info`, matching `PAGE_CANONICAL_MISSING`. Google resolves relative canonicals
exactly as a browser does, so the form is advice rather than a defect — their
canonicalization doc is nonetheless explicit ("Use absolute paths rather than
relative paths with the rel=canonical link element"), the failure it warns about
being a crawled staging copy canonicalizing to itself instead of to production.

Ruleset `baseline` per ADR-009 / SITE-eoqgkcij: canonical is not a sitemaps.org
concept, so this is a consistency diagnostic carrying **no engine verdict** —
never dressed as a spec violation.

### Verification

`Rscript tools/verify.R` OK (docs, registry, lint, check). Registry guard: 94
codes, 74 active, all matched to emitters. Full suite 3893 pass / 0 fail. The one
R CMD check NOTE is the pre-existing new-submission note in `cran-comments.md`.

Two existing tests were updated rather than worked around: a relative canonical
pointing elsewhere now legitimately emits two codes, so they select the mismatch
row instead of asserting a single-element vector.

### Known cross-port behavioral divergence (not reconciled)

Base-URL resolution of a scheme-looking relative reference differs:
`://nonsense` is a valid *relative* reference under the WHATWG URL Standard
(path, no scheme), so the TypeScript port resolves it as a browser does, while
`xml2::url_absolute()` returns NA here and `page_html_canonicals()` takes its
fallback. Recorded on `SMV-dhrpsgvo`. The fallback behavior itself agrees.


### Comments

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Landed on chore/site-nlptpmdq-crossport-verify as 6b59bad. Local only — the GitHub remote is suspended (403), so no push/PR. Bundle refreshed.

Refines the port this issue delivered. `page_canonical_relative_finding()` now requires `identical(f$channel, "html_link")` alongside `isTRUE(f$relative)`, so only a `<link rel="canonical">` element earns `PAGE_CANONICAL_RELATIVE`.

## SITE-koqdjmte: Cross-port subject_ref grammar redesign (contract decision, both ports)

**Status:** done | **Parent:** nlptpmdqqvmldzbdrfwhwlceepjoksne

### Description

### Why this is its own issue

Split out of SITE-ppojfsed by user decision (2026-07-29). SITE-ppojfsed proposed
declaring sitemapr's subject_ref form the winner over the validator's. That was
rejected: the PRINCIPLE is right (anchor to the parent, identify the child
semantically) but sitemapr's current representation has defects of its own, so
adopting it as-is would enshrine them across both ports.

This is a shared cross-port contract migration, not a bug fix, and it is broader
than the index-child case that surfaced it.

### The divergence

    sitemapr   sitemap://<host>/<path>#index-child:<child-url>
    validator  sitemap#index-entry:<n>

Two differences at once: the fragment name, and its payload (child URL vs
positional ordinal). It is an instance of a whole-contract divergence rather
than a per-code one — validator refs are `sitemap#...` throughout while
sitemapr's carry a `sitemap://` authority base.

### Defects in sitemapr's current form (why it is not simply adopted)

1. **Scheme collision.** `sitemap_subject_ref()` (R/protocol-validate.R:134-139)
   strips the scheme outright: `sub("^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9+.-]*://", "", url)`. So
   `http://example.com/s.xml` and `https://example.com/s.xml` both become
   `sitemap://example.com/s.xml`. Two genuinely different documents collapse to
   one ref.
2. **Ambiguous grammar.** A raw child URL is embedded inside a fragment without
   encoding. A child URL may itself contain `#`, so the ref cannot be parsed
   back into (base, fragment, payload) unambiguously.
3. **Cannot address duplicate occurrences.** A child URL alone does not
   distinguish two duplicate `<loc>` entries in one index. The validator's
   ordinal can. This matters directly: sitemapr now emits PROTOCOL_DUPLICATE_LOC
   on index children (319f755), so the two findings it raises for a repeated
   child share one subject_ref.
4. **Index base divergence.** The validator uses ZERO-based indexes while
   sitemapr documents one-based (`#entry:<n>`, findings-contract.md:82). Any
   ordinal-bearing form has to settle this, so the migration is wider than the
   index-child fragment alone.

### Approved target shape (user, 2026-07-29)

Parent URL retaining its ACTUAL scheme, plus a one-based ordinal AND an encoded
child URL — the ordinal makes it addressable, the URL keeps it readable:

    https://example.com/index.xml#index-child:3:<percent-encoded-child-url>

### Done

Grammar specified in findings-contract.md (including the scheme-preserving base,
percent-encoding rule, and one-based ordinal, applied consistently across ALL
fragment kinds, not just index-child); both ports migrated deliberately;
compatibility coverage for persisted validator reports written in the old form;
corpus golden re-derived.

### Files

- `R/protocol-validate.R` — `sitemap_subject_ref()`, `protocol_ref_fragment()`,
  `index_child_refs()`
- `R/validate-sitemap.R` — `index_findings_from_problems()`,
  `index_budget_subject_ref()`
- `docs/findings-contract.md` — the subject_ref scheme and fragment table
- Sibling: `sitemap-validator`, and its counterpart of SMV-dhrpsgvo

### Comments

#### 2026-07-30 — bartek@turczynski.pl

DONE on the sitemapr side at cd0af75. Verify gate green; full suite green; BOTH corpus goldens unmoved (the grammar changes refs, not codes).

Implemented the approved shape and applied the three rules to EVERY fragment kind rather than patching index-child alone, as the Done criteria required: base keeps the document's actual scheme, every URL/path payload is percent-encoded over UTF-8 bytes (RFC 3986 unreserved set, uppercase hex), every ordinal one-based.

All four listed defects are fixed and each is pinned by a test that DEMONSTRATES it rather than merely asserting the new string:
  1. scheme collision — http and https bases now differ; asserted with expect_false(identical(...))
  2. ambiguous grammar — the migrated test whose child URL ends '#part' now shows %23part, and a new test splits a ref carrying '#part:2' back into exactly (base, kind, ordinal, payload)
  3. duplicate addressing — the migrated duplicate-index-child test now reads index-child:2, and a new test asserts two duplicate children get distinguishable refs
  4. index base — one-based is now a rule of the GRAMMAR, stated once, not a property of one fragment

DESIGN POINTS worth recording, since two were not in the issue:

* ONE definition. index_child_subject_ref() is now used by all five emitters (protocol lastmod, protocol locs via index_child_refs, classification feed children, index-expansion scope, index_findings_from_problems). Previously each pasted its own string, which is how the grammar could drift between layers.

* THE ORDINAL IS NOT ALWAYS KNOWABLE — and the reason is structural, not effort. Two of the five emitters read the traversal problems table, which records a child that may sit arbitrarily deep BELOW the base (the traversal root). Its position IN THE BASE DOCUMENT does not exist to be recorded. Those render '-', a fixed-arity marker for 'position not established', rather than a shorter ref a parser would have to guess at. Plumbing an ordinal there would mean inventing one.

* LOCAL PATHS. 'Parent URL retaining its ACTUAL scheme' has no answer for a local file, which has no scheme. Rejected file://: a relative path has no correct authority form and an absolute one makes refs machine-dependent (they would differ per checkout, and the corpus runner passes local paths). The path is used verbatim and the contract says so.

* THE ENCODER IS DELIBERATELY NOT utils::URLencode(). URLencode returns its input UNCHANGED when it already contains a %XX, which would make the encoding non-total and reintroduce exactly the ambiguity rule 2 exists to remove. Pinned by a test asserting 'a%2Fb' -> 'a%252Fb'.

* The acceptance scenario asserting refs begin with 'sitemap://' was rewritten to assert what it was for — the ref anchors to the document's own identifier. Its fixtures are LOCAL files, so under the new grammar their base is the path; a fixed scheme prefix was testing the wrapper, not the anchoring.

COMPATIBILITY: sitemapr composes refs and never parses one — verified, there is no reader anywhere in R/ — so no shim is shipped here and none is needed. The 'compatibility coverage for persisted validator reports' item in the Done criteria belongs to the sibling, which does persist reports (src/lib/db/repositories/report.ts). The generations are cleanly distinguishable: only the old sitemapr form begins 'sitemap://', and the old validator form is exactly 'sitemap#index-entry:<n>'.

CROSS-REPO: filed SMV-olrunnos. Flagged there that rule 3 is the quiet one — the validator's index is ZERO-based, so every ordinal shifts by one — and that it should decide explicitly whether this rides FINDINGS_CONTRACT_VERSION '2' or mints a new generation, coordinating with SMV-wvrfpsve.

Remaining for this issue: only the sibling half (SMV-olrunnos). The sitemapr side is complete.

## SITE-kqnnnvyr: A UTF-16 sitemap raises instead of producing a finding (cross-port divergence)

**Status:** done | **Parent:** nlptpmdqqvmldzbdrfwhwlceepjoksne

### Description

### Claim

A UTF-16-encoded sitemap makes `validate_sitemap()` RAISE rather than return the findings contract. The corpus records this as an accepted limitation (encoding/utf16-le-bom.xml is pinned at `!sitemapr_xml_parse_error` in corpus-golden.tsv, and test-corpus-fixtures.R names UTF-16 among the documented classed-error cases).

The TS port does not raise: it decodes with `decodeUtf8Strict()` = `TextDecoder("utf-8", {fatal:true})` and turns the failure into a finding via `getNonUtf8XmlReason()` (src/lib/services/parsing/parsing/utf8.ts, xml-parser.ts).

### The decision this needs

docs/findings-registry.csv marks BOTH candidate codes `validator-only`:

- ENCODING_NOT_UTF8 (error, classification, source)
- ENCODING_BOM_DETECTED (info, classification, source)

So the divergence may be deliberate -- but if so, 'sitemapr raises where the validator reports' should be written down as a conscious contract difference rather than sitting in a golden file as an unexplained `!sitemapr_xml_parse_error`. Three options:

1. Activate ENCODING_NOT_UTF8 and return a finding (closest to the sibling; makes the two ports joinable on this input).
2. Keep raising, but with a purpose-built classed condition and a documented rationale in findings-contract.md.
3. Keep as-is and record the divergence in the reconcile column of the registry.

Cheapest correct answer is probably (1): the machinery is already there -- `classification_source_finding()` and the classification layer both exist, and the registry row is already written.

### Verify first (epic rule)

Confirm the current behavior before changing anything. Note that encoding/utf16-le-bom.xml is a MISLABELED fixture (UTF-16 BOM followed by plain ASCII), so it exercises the XML-parse failure and NOT a genuine UTF-16 decode. A real UTF-16 document takes a different path -- and today hits SITE-ctkdkuna (the sniffer's bare base R error) before reaching the parser at all. SITE-ctkdkuna must land first or the verification is measuring the wrong crash.

### Depends on

SITE-ctkdkuna -- a genuine UTF-16 document cannot even be sniffed today.

### Done

The behavior for a genuine UTF-16 sitemap is deliberate, documented, and consistent across validate/read/audit; if a code is activated, the registry drift guard and the cross-port reconcile column agree.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

UNBLOCKED, and the premise has SHIFTED — re-verify before implementing. Its dependency SITE-ctkdkuna is fixed at 0fea549.

Re-probed a genuine UTF-16LE sitemap (BOM FF FE + UTF-16LE-encoded urlset, 312 bytes) at 0fea549:

  sniff_format     -> 'xml-urlset'
  validate_sitemap -> RETURNS, 1 finding
  read_sitemap     -> RETURNS, 1 row, loc = https://example.com/a (correct)
  audit_sitemap    -> RETURNS a sitemap_audit

So the issue's headline — 'a UTF-16 sitemap raises here but becomes a finding in the sibling' — no longer holds. It raised only because the SNIFFER crashed on the interleaved NULs before anything could classify it (that was SITE-ctkdkuna). With that gone, UTF-16 parses correctly end to end and does become a finding.

Which means the decision this issue was waiting on — whether to activate ENCODING_NOT_UTF8 / ENCODING_BOM_DETECTED, both registry-marked validator-only — is now a narrower question than 'how do we stop raising'. It is purely: does sitemapr want to REPORT that a document is UTF-16 at all, given that it already reads it correctly? The 'we currently fail' argument for activating them is gone.

But the finding it currently produces is WRONG: ENCODING_BOM_DECLARATION_CONFLICT, on 'encoding="UTF-16"' + a UTF-16LE BOM, which is the canonical conformant form per XML 1.0 SS4.3.3. Filed as SITE-zarjabyz (high, under the epic). That should land BEFORE any decision here — the correct baseline behavior for a UTF-16 sitemap is 'no findings', and it is hard to argue about which encoding codes to add on top of a false positive.

Suggested sequencing: SITE-zarjabyz first, then re-open the validator-only question here against clean output.

No code written for this issue.

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Unblocked further by SITE-zarjabyz (2e2464c): the false positive is gone, so the baseline for a canonical UTF-16 sitemap is now genuinely 'no findings' - confirmed end to end through validate_sitemap() (0 rows) with read_sitemap() returning 1 correct row.

Two facts that bear on this issue's premise before any work starts here:

1. The 'we currently raise on UTF-16' argument is dead. A real UTF-16LE document with encoding="UTF-16" parses fine.
2. encoding/utf16-le-bom.xml is misleading as evidence. Despite the name it is a UTF-16LE BOM over an ASCII/UTF-8 body declaring encoding="UTF-8" - malformed, and its parse error is correct behavior, not a UTF-16 handling gap.

So the case for activating ENCODING_NOT_UTF8 / ENCODING_BOM_DETECTED has to be made on its own merits (informational parity with the sibling port), not on a defect. Apply the epic's step-1 rule accordingly.

#### 2026-07-30 — bartek@turczynski.pl

DONE at b1d1433. Verify gate green (docs, registry, lint, R CMD check 1 NOTE = the pre-existing URL-404 note from the account suspension).

STEP 1 (verify first) — re-confirmed the prior comments' baseline at HEAD before touching anything: a genuine UTF-16LE sitemap (FF FE + UTF-16LE body declaring encoding="UTF-16") sniffs as xml-urlset, validates with 0 findings, reads 1 correct row. The 'we raise on UTF-16' premise was indeed dead.

DECISION: option (1) — activate ENCODING_NOT_UTF8, and ALSO ENCODING_BOM_DETECTED. But the argument is NOT parity, which matters because the last comment correctly said the parity case had to stand on its own merits. The real ground is sitemapr's OWN spec doc: docs/sitemap-spec.md §12.5 baseline requires a UTF-8 file (from §2/§4/§7), and its BOM row already states that a non-UTF-8 leading mark errors. So a UTF-16 sitemap was an unenforced documented rule, not a cosmetic gap. Reading a document successfully is not the same as the document being conformant.

RULE SHAPE — read the sibling's code rather than the issue's paraphrase, which changed the design. getNonUtf8XmlReason() (src/lib/services/parsing/utf8.ts) is a three-tier cascade: non-UTF-8 BOM, then a non-UTF-8 XML-declaration LABEL via isUtf8EncodingLabel(), then strict byte decode. It is a LABEL test for tiers 1-2, and that is essential, not incidental: a pure byte test cannot see a UTF-16 document at all, because UTF-16LE ASCII is bytes below 0x80 interleaved with NULs and every one is a valid UTF-8 sequence (U+0000 included). Strict UTF-8 decoding ACCEPTS a UTF-16LE body. The reason the sibling catches it is that the FF FE mark itself is invalid UTF-8. sitemapr mirrors the cascade tier for tier, plus one documented superset tier (HTTP Content-Type charset, below the declaration, per its own §3/§11.6 priority — unobservable in the corpus, which is local files with no response).

CORPUS GOLDEN: exactly 4 rows moved, nothing else.
  encoding/utf8-bom.xml                <none> -> ENCODING_BOM_DETECTED           CONVERGES
  encoding/declared-iso8859-no-bom.xml <none> -> ENCODING_NOT_UTF8               CONVERGES
  encoding/bom-conflict.xml            +BOM_DETECTED +NOT_UTF8                   CONVERGES
  text/utf8-bom.txt                    <none> -> ENCODING_BOM_DETECTED           DIVERGES
The third is worth reading twice: a UTF-8 BOM over a declared ISO-8859-1. The BOM wins the RESOLUTION (so the file is UTF-8) and the declaration still fires NOT_UTF8. Not a contradiction — a declaration that lies about the encoding is a genuine defect, and the sibling's tier 2 fires there too.

DIVERGENCE, deliberate and filed as SMV-luydhpej: the sibling emits BOM_DETECTED only from validateXmlProtocol(), so its TEXT path never reports a mark. sitemapr's classification layer runs once per source and is format-agnostic by construction; branching it on format to reproduce what looks like an omission would push format knowledge into a layer that has none. So text/utf8-bom.txt is not a golden join row.

SITE-zarjabyz PRESERVED, not reversed: its test is narrowed to what it actually claimed (the canonical UTF-16 spelling emits no BOM/declaration CONFLICT) and now also asserts NOT_UTF8 + BOM_DETECTED. The mark and the declaration agree with each other; both disagree with the protocol.

Registry: both rows flipped validator-only -> active with reconcile=done; active count 74 -> 76, validator-only 20 -> 18, doc counts updated. Both registry copies + the published revision/digest bumped (the guard added in SITE-xptyuczr forced that, as designed).

Docs: sitemap-spec.md §3 now separates conflict RESOLUTION from CONFORMANCE; findings-contract.md gains an 'Encoding codes: what agrees and what does not' subsection recording both asymmetries; NEWS announces both codes.

### Description

### E.1b: refactor E.5 into a consultable robots facts/decisions producer (§7)

Governing: `docs/design/layer-e-page-inspection.md` §7, §5.4, §0.3, §0.8.

**Problem:** `validate_robots()` (`R/robots-validate.R:161`) returns **findings only** — allowed URLs produce no row and the decisions object is discarded, so the §5.4 synthesis can't consult E.5. It also calls the **legacy Google-only** facade `robotstxtr::allowed_by_robots_url()` (line 167).

#### Decision
- Extract robots evaluation into an internal **facts/decisions producer** returning a per-URL decision object (mapping onto ADR-009 §2 outcome fields); derive **both** the `ROBOTS_*` findings **and** the §5.4 synthesis input from it.
- **Route through `robots_evaluate_url_v1(url, robots_product_token, robots_policy_ruleset, matcher_backend, …)`** so the axes + `matcher_status`/availability flow through (enables the per-engine synthesis gate in E.3, §0.3).

- Gate any synthesis consumer on robots evaluation being **enabled and available** (`check_robots = TRUE` **and** `robotstxtr` present).

- `robotstxtyandex` is **batch-shaped** (not row-dispatchable) — a `robotstxtr` integration detail to respect if exercising the Yandex backend.

#### Blocks
E.3 (synthesis); the §0.6 sitemap-blocked check (consultable decision).

---
#### Round-2 hardening delta (§0.3, §0.9)
- **Explicit robots-axis carrier (not silent derivation).** This producer needs `robots_policy_ruleset` + `matcher_backend` as **explicit** inputs — `ruleset_context()` carries only the four sitemap-source axes today. Deriving them from `sitemap_ruleset` violates ADR-009 independence; add explicit args / a structured robots context with documented presets whose expanded values are retained.
- **Public capability accessor:** `robots_engine_contract_v1()$matcher_capability` (`engine_backend_capability_v1()` is internal).

## SITE-lcmvzpel: Text path: no duplicate detection, no count cap, no NUL in URI-illegal set

**Status:** done | **Parent:** nlptpmdqqvmldzbdrfwhwlceepjoksne

### Description

### Claim

Three gaps in the text-sitemap path relative to the sibling's `parseTextSitemap()` (`src/lib/services/parsing/text-parser.ts:79-273`):

1. **No duplicate-`<loc>` detection** — the sibling keys a `seenUrls` set and emits `PROTOCOL_DUPLICATE_LOC`. sitemapr's `validate_url_count()` (`R/protocol-validate.R:314`) operates on the XML rows path only.
2. **No per-file URL count cap** — the sibling applies `maxUrls: 50_000` on the text path (`pipeline.ts:502`).
3. **No per-line SSRF check** — the sibling calls `checkUrlSafety` per line with `SSRF_HOSTNAMES` / `SSRF_IP_PREFIXES` (`text-parser.ts:40-45`).

Line-level diagnostics are otherwise near-parity: `validate_text_protocol()` (`R/protocol-validate.R:1972+`) covers `PROTOCOL_TEXT_BLANK_LINE`, `PROTOCOL_URL_NOT_ABSOLUTE`, `PROTOCOL_URL_NO_HOST`, and `PROTOCOL_TEXT_URL_TOO_LONG` at the same 2,048 threshold.

Separately, and trivially: sitemapr's URI-illegal character class starts at `\x01` (`R/protocol-validate.R:165-167`), so a **NUL byte** is not caught; the sibling covers `\x00-\x1f` (`src/lib/services/protocol/xml-protocol.ts:45`).

### Step 1 — Verify before coding (REQUIRED)

1. Run a text sitemap with a repeated URL, one with 60,000 lines, and one containing `http://169.254.169.254/`. Record what fires for each.
2. For the SSRF item, establish the layer question first: sitemapr already guards SSRF at *fetch* time (`R/ssrf.R`, `fetch_hop_ssrf_guard()`). A per-line check in the parser is a **reporting** feature — telling the user their sitemap lists an internal address — not a safety control. **Confirm the fetch-time guard covers the actual safety case** before adding a parser-level check, and frame the finding accordingly.
3. Confirm the NUL claim with a `\x00`-containing `<loc>`.

### Why it matters

Duplicates and the count cap are straightforward parity gaps on a format sitemapr fully supports. The SSRF item is informational value, not a hole — do not overstate it.

### Approach

Reuse the existing codes (`PROTOCOL_DUPLICATE_LOC`, `PROTOCOL_URL_COUNT_EXCEEDED`) rather than minting text-specific variants; the sibling reuses them too, which keeps the corpus goldens joinable. The NUL fix is a one-character change to the character class plus a test.

### Files

- `R/protocol-validate.R` — `validate_text_protocol()`, URI-illegal class
- `tests/testthat/`

### Done

Duplicate and over-count text sitemaps emit the shared codes; the NUL byte is caught; the SSRF layering decision is recorded on the issue whichever way it goes.


### Comments

#### 2026-07-28 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

VERIFIED — SPLIT RESULT (2026-07-29): items 1 and 2 confirmed, the NUL item does not reproduce and is unreachable by construction.

CONFIRMED (1) duplicate detection: a 3-line text sitemap with one URL repeated -> zero findings. No PROTOCOL_DUPLICATE_LOC.
CONFIRMED (2) count cap: a 60,000-line text sitemap -> zero findings. No PROTOCOL_URL_COUNT_EXCEEDED. Both gaps are real; validate_url_count() is XML-rows-only as described.

DOES NOT REPRODUCE (4) NUL byte: extending the URI-illegal class from \x01 to \x00 would be dead code. A NUL can never reach has_uri_illegal_char() on either path:
- text path: rawToChar() raises "embedded nul in string" during text_as_string(), before any validation
- XML path: libxml2 rejects it at parse — raw byte gives "Invalid character: Char 0x0 out of allowed range", and the &#0; charref gives "xmlParseCharRef: invalid xmlChar value 0". NUL is not a legal XML character at all (XML 1.0 section 2.2), so no conforming or non-conforming XML document can carry one into a <loc>.
Recommend dropping item 4 rather than "fixing" it, and noting the reason in a code comment at R/protocol-validate.R:165-167 so the class boundary is not re-flagged by the next comparison run.

(3) SSRF-per-line: layering question unchanged, still to be recorded. Deferring it to its own decision rather than bundling with the two confirmed parity gaps.

Any caller feeding fetched bytes to parse_sitemap_text() gets an unclassed error it cannot dispatch on. Filing separately.

## SITE-lgpgudfb: Harden SSRF guard: NAT64 + IPv4-translated + exotic IPv6->v4 prefixes

**Status:** done | **Parent:** efrzatkbtlgzngmdotjyeucprxrqoyaj

### Description

Post-v1 hardening beyond ADR-003's enumerated matrix. The v1 structural SSRF guard (R/ssrf.R, SITE-vjbhhuru) covers ::ffff: IPv4-mapped (dotted + hex-hextet). It does NOT decode other IPv6->IPv4 embedding prefixes that can also reach internal v4 ranges: NAT64 (64:ff9b::/96 and the configurable 64:ff9b:1::/48), IPv4-translated (::ffff:0:0:0/96, i.e. ::ffff:0:a.b.c.d), and deprecated SIIT forms. Also consider DNS resolve-then-check (explicitly deferred in ADR-003 §1). Revisit when tightening the guard for production; update ADR-003 matrix accordingly.

### Comments

#### 2026-06-28 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Probed rurl normalization of IPv6 embedding forms. Findings: rurl is inconsistent — it hex-normalizes some dotted tails (64:ff9b::127.0.0.1 -> 64:ff9b::7f00:1, is_ip=TRUE) but leaves others dotted (::127.0.0.1, 64:ff9b::8.8.8.8, is_ip=FALSE). So the guard must decode every spelling itself. Plan: replace the two single-purpose ::ffff: tail helpers with a unified ssrf_ipv6_hextets() expander (8 numeric hextets, handles ::, dotted tails, hex) + ssrf_embedded_ipv4() that recognizes mapped/translated/compatible/NAT64-WKP(/96)/NAT64-local(/48 per RFC 6052) and checks the embedded v4 against blocked ranges (public embeds still allowed, consistent with existing ipv4-mapped). New reason codes: ipv4-translated, ipv4-compatible, nat64.

#### 2026-06-28 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Done — merged in PR #13 (squash, commit b613ff2 on main).

Implementation: replaced the two ::ffff:-only tail helpers with a unified ssrf_ipv6_hextets() expander (8 numeric hextets; handles ::, dotted-quad tails, hex, fully-expanded forms) + ssrf_embedded_ipv4() that detects each embedding prefix by bit position and re-runs ssrf_classify_ipv4() on the embedded v4. Public embeds still pass, consistent with the existing ipv4-mapped policy.

Coverage added beyond v1: IPv4-translated (::ffff:0:0:0/96 -> 'ipv4-translated'), deprecated IPv4-compatible (::/96 -> 'ipv4-compatible', excludes ::/::1), NAT64 WKP (64:ff9b::/96 -> 'nat64'), NAT64 local-use (64:ff9b:1::/48 -> 'nat64', decoded per RFC 6052 §2.2 around the reserved u-byte). All dotted/hex/expanded spellings handled since rurl normalizes them inconsistently.

Also corrected a prior test that misread ::ffff:1 as mapped 0.0.0.1 (it is the plain address 0:0:0:0:0:0:ffff:1). ADR-003 §1 matrix updated. DNS resolve-then-check and arbitrary deployment NAT64 prefixes left out of scope per ADR-003 rationale (CRAN offline, library threat model).

## SITE-lwvktkte: report.R drops page/robots-layer findings (report_layer_order omits them)

**Status:** done

### Description

### Bug

`report_layer_order` in `R/report.R:44` lists only:

    input, fetch, discovery, classification, decompression, schema, protocol, index-expansion, report

It omits the **`page`** and **`robots`** layers. The findings renderer filters findings to that list:

    present_layers <- report_layer_order[report_layer_order %in% findings$layer]   # R/report.R:591

so any finding whose `layer` is `page` or `robots` is silently dropped from the HTML report — no section, no row, no error.

### Impact (already live, not hypothetical)

This is a shipped-code bug, independent of the in-flight Layer E epic:

- E.5 robots allow/disallow shipped in PR #134. `validate_sitemap(check_robots = TRUE)` emits `robots`-layer findings (`ROBOTS_DISALLOWED`, `ROBOTS_INDETERMINATE`; `layer = "robots"` per findings-contract.md:59). Those findings **do not render in the report today** — they pass through the pipeline and are filtered out at report time.
- It also blocks the rest of Layer E: any future `page`-layer finding (`PAGE_*`) would be dropped the same way. This is called out as a precondition in the Layer E spec (_scratch/layer-e-page-inspection-spec.md §6.3) and epic SITE-ihycidfl.

The canonical layer order is `findings_layer_order` in `R/findings-assemble.R:17`, which **does** include `page` and `robots` in the right positions (after `index-expansion`, before `report`). `report_layer_order` has simply drifted from it.

### Fix

Add `page` and `robots` to `report_layer_order` (`R/report.R:44`), between `index-expansion` and `report`, matching `findings_layer_order`. The comment at R/report.R:42-43 already claims it mirrors `findings_layer_order` — the two must be kept in lockstep (consider a test asserting equality of the two vectors so this can't drift again).

### Verify

- Add a fixture/test: `validate_sitemap(check_robots = TRUE)` on a sitemap advertising a robots-disallowed URL → build the report → assert the `ROBOTS_DISALLOWED` finding renders (a robots section is present).
- Regression guard: assert `report_layer_order == findings_layer_order` (or that report order is a permutation covering every findings layer).

## SITE-mgjfbigc: Resolve operation_free_requests(): wire it into the throttle or delete it with its tautological test

**Status:** done

### Description

R/fetch.R:597. operation_free_requests(state) returns 0L for a NULL state and 1L otherwise -- unconditionally. Nothing in R/ calls it; the only callers are tests/testthat/test-concurrency-contract.R:217 and tests/testthat/test-fetch.R:979, and both assert exactly the constant the function hardcodes. The pair is circular: it proves the literal, not that the throttle actually grants one free request per operation.

Its comment says it 'surfaces that store-level invariant' from ADR-008 section 6 (ONE per-host throttle store threaded through discovery and every index expansion, so one operation gets ONE free request, not one per phase). That invariant is real and worth asserting -- the question is whether it is asserted anywhere that would fail if the pacing code regressed.

Two ways out, pick one:
(a) Wire it in -- have the real pacing path derive its free-request budget through this function, so the tests become load-bearing.
(b) Delete the function and both tests, and instead assert the invariant behaviorally: drive a fetch across a discovery + index-expansion sequence and count un-paced requests to one host.

(b) is likelier the honest fix; (a) only pays off if the budget ever becomes non-constant. Coverage is 100% either way -- the function currently only stays covered because its own tests call it.

Found in the /cran grooming pass (see SITE-etpxaqkd); left alone there because it is a design call, not a mechanical cleanup.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-28 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Resolved via option (b): deleted operation_free_requests() and both tautological tests (commit 4008a8d on chore/site-mgjfbigc-drop-free-requests).

Rationale: the behavioral assertion option (b) called for already exists and is load-bearing. test-concurrency-contract.R "sitemap_tree paces all phases against one shared bucket" drives discovery (guessed-path catalog) plus index expansion through one shared throttle store on a virtual clock and asserts length(slept) == n_requests - 1L -- i.e. exactly ONE un-paced request across the whole operation. If a phase built its own store, the sleep count would drop and that test fails. The throttle-off (NULL state) half is covered by test-fetch.R "the default (throttle = NULL) policy paces nothing". So no new test was needed; only the circular pair had to go.

Option (a) rejected: the budget has no path to becoming non-constant, so routing the real pacing code through a function that always returns 1L would be indirection without a payload.

## SITE-mhfmtdxa: Harden the link-local and cloud-metadata IPv6 rules: they match the literal, not the expanded address

**Status:** done

### Description

Deferred out of SITE-vovtwvuh. That ticket fixed the same class of defect for
the two all-zero-prefix specials (`::1`, `::`) by deciding them on the
**expanded** hextets. The remaining two IPv6 rules in `ssrf_classify_ipv6()`
(`R/ssrf.R`, ~lines 292-299) still match **regex against the literal string**,
and both fail — in opposite directions.

It was deliberately left out of scope there: sitemapr's guard is a copy of
robotstxtr's, and SITE-vovtwvuh existed to keep the two in step. Fixing only
one copy is the exact drift that ticket was preventing. So this must land in
both repos, or the shared-code question below must be settled first.

### Confirmed empirically (main @ ae28c5e, via `ssrf_classify_ipv6()`)

```
fd00:ec2::254             -> cloud-metadata
fd00:0ec2::254            -> NA          <-- BYPASS: same address, allowed
fd00:0ec2:0:0:0:0:0:0254  -> NA          <-- BYPASS: same address, allowed

fe80::1                   -> link-local  (correct)
fe8::                     -> link-local  <-- OVER-BLOCK: hextet is 0x0fe8
fe8:0:0:0:0:0:0:1         -> link-local  <-- OVER-BLOCK
feb::                     -> link-local  <-- OVER-BLOCK
fea:                      -> link-local  <-- OVER-BLOCK
```

`ssrf_classify_literal()` returns `ssrf_result(is.na(reason), reason)`, so an
`NA` classification means **allowed**. The cloud-metadata rows above are a real
SSRF bypass of the AWS metadata block, not a cosmetic mismatch.

### Root cause

1. **cloud-metadata (under-blocks).** The rule is
   `low == "fd00:ec2::254" || grepl("^fd00:ec2:", low)`. A hextet may be written
   with leading zeros, so `0ec2` is the same 16 bits as `ec2` but does not match
   the literal prefix.
2. **link-local (over-blocks).** The rule is `grepl("^fe[89ab][0-9a-f]?:", low)`,
   whose 4th hex digit is optional. A 3-digit first hextet such as `fe8` is
   `0x0fe8`, which is nowhere near `fe80::/10` (`0xfe80`-`0xfebf`). Note the
   link-local rule has no bypass in the other direction: `fe80` is already four
   significant digits, so no leading-zero spelling of it exists.

### Fix shape

Both rules should read the expanded hextets from `ssrf_ipv6_hextets()`, the same
expander `ssrf_ipv6_special()` and `ssrf_embedded_ipv4()` already use:

- link-local: `h[1]` in `0xfe80..0xfebf` (i.e. `bitwAnd(h[1], 0xffc0) == 0xfe80`)
- cloud-metadata: `h[1] == 0xfd00 && h[2] == 0x0ec2`, then the `::254` host part
  for the exact endpoint vs the `/64` prefix

Add tests for every spelling of both, mirroring the 12-spelling table
SITE-vovtwvuh added for the specials.

### Cross-repo

The identical defect is in robotstxtr's copy of the guard (parity source:
robotstxtr `032d9c3`). Needs a mirrored ticket and a byte-for-byte identical
patch there, landed together with this one.

### Open question raised on SITE-vovtwvuh, still unresolved

Should this guard become **shared code** rather than two copies that can drift?
This is now the second parity fix in a row against the same file. Decide that
before writing a third mirrored patch — the answer changes whether this issue is
one patch or two.


### Comments

#### 2026-07-24 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Cross-repo mirror filed in robotstxtr as ROBO-pjvypcjk. Verified the rules are textually identical there (robotstxtr R/ssrf.R lines 291 and 295), so the defect is present in both copies. Land the two patches together.

#### 2026-07-25 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Fixed and merged as ff1215d (PR #175); all CI checks green, branch deleted local+remote.

Both rules now read the expanded hextets from ssrf_ipv6_hextets():
- link-local: bitwAnd(h[1], 0xffc0) == 0xfe80  (fe80::/10)
- cloud-metadata: h[1] == 0xfd00 && h[2] == 0x0ec2  (fd00:ec2::/32)

This is what the ADR-003 §1 matrix already specified (it names fe80::/10 and fd00:ec2::254) — only the code had drifted, so no ADR change was needed. The /32 breadth matches what the old literal '^fd00:ec2:' match already had, so nothing previously blocked became allowed.

ssrf_classify_ipv6() now expands the literal ONCE and passes hextets to every rule. ssrf_embedded_reason() takes hextets instead of a literal; its unit test was updated to feed it hextets.

Landed byte-for-byte with robotstxtr ROBO-pjvypcjk (6777da2, robotstxtr PR #60); ssrf_ipv6_prefix_block() and ssrf_classify_ipv6() are byte-identical across the two repos, verified by diff.

Open question (shared code vs. two copies) is NOT resolved by this patch — still open for a decision before a third mirrored patch.

#### 2026-07-25 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

OPEN QUESTION NOW SETTLED (2026-07-25, user decision). This issue's cross-repo note said to settle shared-code-vs-copies before writing a third mirrored patch.

## SITE-mnahrdnt: Add search-engine-specific sitemap validation profiles

**Status:** done

### Description

### Problem

`validate_sitemap()` currently treats sitemap location and URL scope primarily as Sitemap Protocol conformance. This is correct for sitemaps.org, but major search engines differ in documented behavior. We need per-search-engine validation profiles so findings can distinguish protocol conformance from practical crawler compatibility.

This was prompted by `https://www.tidio.com/sitemap/sitemap.xml`: child sitemaps under `/sitemap/` list root-level URLs, producing `PROTOCOL_URL_OUT_OF_SCOPE`. That is protocol-relevant, but may not be a Google problem depending on submission path.

### Proposed direction

Introduce an explicit consumer/ruleset concept, separate from `mode = strict/non-strict`.

Possible API shape:

```r
validate_sitemap(
  x,
  profile = c("sitemaps.org", "google", "bing", "yandex"),
  submission = c("unknown", "discovered", "robots_txt", "search_console", "webmaster_tools"),
  mode = c("strict", "non-strict")
)
```

Keep `mode` orthogonal: strictness controls severity/filtering within the selected profile. It should not encode Google/Bing/Yandex behavior.

### Evidence and profile notes

#### sitemaps.org

Baseline protocol profile. Sitemap file location constrains eligible URLs by same host and same-or-lower directory. Current `PROTOCOL_URL_OUT_OF_SCOPE` behavior belongs here, though it may need splitting into more precise rule codes.

Reference: https://www.sitemaps.org/protocol.html

#### Google

Google says sitemap file location matters unless the sitemap is submitted through Search Console. Google also supports cross-site sitemaps for verified properties via Search Console or robots.txt.

Profile implication:

- `submission = "discovered"`: directory scope warning should remain.
- `submission = "search_console"`: directory scope issue may be downgraded or suppressed.
- Cross-site sitemap behavior can be compatible when ownership is verified.
- Relative URLs remain invalid; Google expects fully-qualified absolute URLs.
- Google ignores `<priority>` and `<changefreq>`.

Reference: https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/build-sitemap

#### Bing

Bing has historical but still-hosted documentation for cross-domain sitemap hosting. The key distinction: Bing allows a sitemap to be hosted elsewhere if referenced by the target site robots.txt, but URLs inside that sitemap must belong to the same domain as the robots.txt file. The post also says individual sitemap files should be no larger than 10 MB uncompressed, and duplicate URLs with conflicting metadata cause Bing to disregard metadata and use the URL.

Profile implication:

- Do not simply inherit pure sitemaps.org.
- Allow cross-domain sitemap location when `submission = "robots_txt"` establishes trust.
- Still require listed URLs to belong to the robots.txt domain.
- Consider Bing-specific 10 MB compatibility warning even though protocol permits 50 MB.
- Treat conflicting metadata across duplicate URLs as advisory for Bing.

Reference: https://blogs.bing.com/webmaster/February-2008/Microsoft-to-support-cross-domain-Sitemaps

The downloaded Bing Sitemap Plugin source also provides implementation clues, not definitive policy: it generates standard sitemaps.org XML with a Bing `ssp` extension namespace, percent-encodes non-ASCII and unsafe URL bytes, rolls child sitemap files at 50,000 entries or about 10 MB, filters robots-disallowed URLs, and only keeps canonical URLs on the configured host.

Relevant local research source extracted to `_scratch/bing-sitemap-code/`:

- `merge/SitemapOutput.cpp`: URL encoding, XML output, sitemap index output, 50,000 / 10 MB rollovers.
- `pluginlib/PluginSite.cpp`: same-host canonical filtering, HTTP/content-type/robots filtering.
- `merge/DeltaMerge.cpp`: old ping behavior, not current policy.

#### Yandex

Yandex supports XML and TXT sitemaps, explicitly does not support RSS/Atom as sitemap files, recognizes Cyrillic URLs both original and encoded, requires UTF-8, max 50,000 links, max 50 MB uncompressed, same domain as site, and HTTP 200 OK.

Profile implication:

- Unicode/IRI URL findings should be relaxed or downgraded for Yandex when valid UTF-8/Cyrillic appears.
- RSS/Atom sitemap sources should become Yandex-incompatible even if accepted elsewhere.
- Same-domain rule matters; cross-domain hosting is likely not allowed unless future evidence says otherwise.
- HTTP 200 requirement may be stricter than our current fetch handling for non-entrypoint children.

Reference: https://yandex.com/support/webmaster/en/controlling-robot/sitemap

### Design concern

Current `PROTOCOL_URL_OUT_OF_SCOPE` combines at least two concepts:

1. Sitemap file location scope: where the sitemap is hosted relative to the URLs it describes.
2. Listed URL ownership/scope: whether entries belong to the relevant host/domain/property.

For profiles, these likely need distinct findings, for example:

- `PROTOCOL_SITEMAP_LOCATION_OUT_OF_SCOPE`
- `PROTOCOL_URL_OUT_OF_SCOPE`
- `ENGINE_CROSS_SUBMISSION_REQUIRES_ROBOTS`
- `ENGINE_SIZE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`
- `ENGINE_UNSUPPORTED_SITEMAP_FORMAT`

Exact names should be decided during design.

### Acceptance criteria

- Add a documented profile/ruleset design that separates protocol conformance from search-engine compatibility.
- Preserve the existing default behavior unless an explicit profile is selected, or make any default change deliberate and documented.
- Add tests for Google directory-scope handling by submission mode.
- Add tests for Bing robots.txt cross-domain hosting behavior and same-domain URL requirement.
- Add tests for Yandex Cyrillic/original Unicode URL handling and RSS/Atom incompatibility.
- Update findings registry and docs with profile-specific semantics and evidence links.
- Ensure output remains deterministic and keeps the stable findings tibble contract.

### Open questions

- Should profile-specific findings be separate codes, or should existing codes carry a `profile`/`ruleset` context?
- Should `profile = "all"` emit parallel findings for multiple engines?
- How should verified ownership be represented locally: explicit `submission` only, robots.txt discovery, user-provided verified domains, or a combination?
- Should profile support live robots.txt checks, or only evaluate based on provided context for reproducibility?


### Comments

#### 2026-07-16 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Coordination note ahead of the docs/sitemap-spec.md §12 extension (governed by ADR-009).

1. Bing size limit — the Bing section above says 'no larger than 10 MB uncompressed'. That is the obsolete 2008 value and must NOT enter the Bing ruleset. Current Bing = 50 MB (2016 announcement, restated by current help + the Jul-2025 post); it supersedes the 2008 10 MB and the 2009 XML-only statement (SMP-POL-006).

2. Canonical size value = 52,428,800 bytes (50 MiB = 50x1024x1024), per sitemaps.org verbatim ('no larger than 50MB (52,428,800 bytes)', both file and index), matched by Google/Bing. NOT the round 50,000,000. sitemapr is correct (R/protocol-validate.R:250 = 52428800L; sitemap-spec.md §2). sitemap-validator was wrong (pipeline.ts:481 = 50_000_000) -> filed high-priority SMV-idhjmljf.

3. The 'profile = c(...)' / 'submission = c("unknown","discovered","robots_txt",...)' ## SITE-ndwnfyer: ADR: opt-in page inspection — network expansion, budget & page-fetch contract (D5+D7)

**Status:** done | **Parent:** ihycidflmgtcvnctecfqldgdulicucex

### Description

### ADR: opt-in page inspection — network expansion, budget & page-fetch contract

Governing: `docs/design/layer-e-page-inspection.md` §0.2, §0.4, §3.

Write `docs/decisions/ADR-01x-page-inspection.md` covering:

#### 1. Opt-in network expansion
Page inspection fetches advertised **page bodies** — a deliberate, **default-off** network expansion (v1 never did). Own budget + API surface (E.1f Contract D). NOT an ADR-007 exception (ADR-007 only constrains `probe_url()` resolving sitemap *children*); justified on its own terms (opt-in + budget + default-off).

#### 2. Page-fetch body contract — **amends ADR-009 §2** (not a cross-ref)
- Add `partial` to the `evidence_status` enum: an **intentional prefix-acquisition window** (body truncated at the per-page cap, head-region facts usable), **distinct from `incomplete`** (no usable body). Accepted ADR-009 currently maps a reached body ceiling to `incomplete`; this ADR overrides that for the intentional page cap. This is an explicit ADR-009 amendment.
- Add an **ADR-003 page-cap subsection**: the per-page cap (single-MB) is **truncate-and-retain**; ADR-003's 500 MB ceiling stays the outer **discard** backstop.

#### 3. Safety & resource precedence
- SSRF / scheme / HTTPS→HTTP downgrade → `safety_refused` → `PAGE_SSRF_BLOCKED`.
- **500 MB resource-ceiling discard → `PAGE_FETCH_FAILED`** (resource/transport failure), **not** `PAGE_SSRF_BLOCKED` (§0.5). Keep resource refusal and SSRF distinct.

#### Blocks
E.1a (fetch artifact + safety precedence). No dependencies.

---
#### Round-2 hardening delta (§0.4) — CORRECTION on `partial`
`partial` is **already** in the ADR-009 §2 `evidence_status` enum (ADR-009:104) — do **not** "add" it. This ADR must instead:
- **(a)** amend the **ADR-009 §3 body-ceiling rule** (accepted ADR-009 resolves a reached body ceiling to `incomplete`; the intentional truncate-and-retain page cap resolves to `partial`);
- **(b)** define the page-cap `partial` semantics;
- **(c)** add an **ADR-003** page-cap subsection.

Name these as **direct edits to ADR-009 §3 and ADR-003**, not an enum addition and not a cross-reference.
